# A sharp open-tail inequality for concave sequences

## 1. Statement

Let `(w_i)` be a finite nonnegative concave sequence on consecutive integer
indices. Suppose its total mass `M` is positive and its weighted mean is an
integer `j`. Put `p=w_j/M`. Then

    sum_(i>j) w_i >= (3/7)(M-w_j),
    sum_(i<j) w_i >= (3/7)(M-w_j).                       (1)

The factor `3/7` is sharp. The sequence `(4,3,2,1)` on indices
`(-1,0,1,2)` has mean zero and right open-tail mass three, while its
noncentral mass is seven. This is a statement about open tails; it is
stronger in a different direction than the closed-tail `4/9` bound.

The proof below consists of a concave-cone dual certificate and explicit
polynomial positivity certificates. All coefficient computations are exact;
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_sharp_open_tail_concave_sequence.py` reproduces them with rational
arithmetic and verifies the sharpness and geometric corollary constants.

## 2. The elementary cone generators

Translate the actual index interval to `0,...,L`, and denote its integer mean
by `a`. A singleton is immediate. Zero end values may be discarded until the
positive support is reached. If at least two positive terms remain, positivity
forces the mean to be strictly between the positive extreme indices, so an
integer mean requires at least three terms. We may therefore take `L>=2` and
`1<=a<=L-1`.

Every nonnegative concave sequence is a nonnegative linear combination of

    A_i=(L-i)/L,   B_i=i/L,
    T_i^j=min(i/j,(L-i)/(L-j)),  1<=j<=L-1.              (2)

Indeed subtract the affine interpolation of its nonnegative endpoint values.
The remaining sequence vanishes at both endpoints and has nonnegative
negative second differences. The discrete Dirichlet Green functions
`G(i,j)=min(i,j)(L-max(i,j))/L` reconstruct it from those differences;
`G(i,j)=j(L-j)T_i^j/L`. This proves (2), including zero curvatures.

For a sequence `v`, write

    D(v)=sum_i(i-a)v_i,
    F(v)=7 sum_(i>a)v_i-3(sum_i v_i-v_a).

To prove the right inequality in (1), it suffices to find a real number
`lambda` with `F(v)>=lambda D(v)` on all generators. The mean condition
then annihilates the right side after adding their nonnegative multiples.

The generator means are

    mean(A)=(L-1)/3,   mean(B)=(2L+1)/3,
    mass(T^j)=L/2,    mean(T^j)=(L+j)/3.                 (3)

These identities follow from the finite sums of integers and squares on the
two sides of the tent. Thus any feasible a satisfies

    L-1 <= 3a <= 2L+1.                                 (4)

If equality holds on the right, all nonzero generator coefficients must be
on B, because its mean is strictly larger than every other generator mean.
For B in that case,

    F(B)=(4L+5)(L-1)/(9L)>=0.

We may henceforth suppose `b:=2L+1-3a>0`. Define

    R=L-a,
    A0=4L(L+1)-7a^2-a,
    lambda=3A0/[L(L+1)b].                              (5)

Here `A0>0`: its minimum over (4) occurs at `a=(2L+1)/3`, where it equals
`2(4L+5)(L-1)/9`. Direct summation gives `F(B)=lambda D(B)`.

## 3. The three residual polynomials

For the left affine generator, multiplication by the positive denominator
`2Lb` gives

    P0=4L^3-28L^2a-4L^2+63La^2+13La-42a^3-6a^2.        (6)

Thus `F(A)-lambda D(A)=P0/(2Lb)`.
For a tent with `j<=a`, one has

    F(T^j)=R(7R-1)/[2(L-j)]-3L/2,
    D(T^j)=L(L+j-3a)/6.

The residual multiplied by `2(L-j)(L+1)b` is

    P=(R(7R-1)-3L(L-j))(L+1)b
                          -(L-j)A0(L+j-3a).            (7)

For a tent with `j>=a`, the analogous formulas are

    F(T^j)=2L-a(7a+1)/(2j),
    Pplus=(4Lj-a(7a+1))(L+1)b-j A0(L+j-3a),             (8)

with residual denominator `2j(L+1)b`.

As a function of j, `Pplus` is concave, with quadratic coefficient `-A0`.
It therefore suffices to check its two endpoints `j=a` and `j=L-1`.
At the former,

    Pplus(a)=a(R+1) G,
    G=4L^2-14La+2L+14a^2-5a-1.

Completing the square gives

    G=14(a-L/2-5/28)^2+(28L^2-28L-81)/56>0   (L>=3).

At the latter,

    Pplus(L-1)=2[4L^3-4L-3a(L-a)(7a+1)].

Since `a^2(L-a)<=4L^3/27` and `a(L-a)<=L^2/4` on `[0,L]`, the bracket is at
least `8L^3/9-3L^2/4-4L`, which is positive for `L>=3`.
When `L=2`, the only relevant integer value is `a=j=1`, and the endpoint
residual is zero. It remains to verify (6) and (7).

## 4. Explicit positivity certificates for P0 and P

First suppose `L>=11`, and set

    L=11+x,   a=(L-1+(L+2)t)/3,   j=1+(a-1)u,
    x>=0,  0<=t<=1,  0<=u<=1.                          (9)

These substitutions cover every real value in (4) and `1<=j<=a`.

Here is the coefficient convention used in the certificate. If a polynomial
on a rectangle, after mapping that rectangle to the unit square, is

    E(x,t,u)=sum c_(k,i,j) x^k t^i u^j,

and its t,u degrees are d,e, its Bernstein coefficients at x degree k are

    B_(k,I,J)=sum_(i<=I,j<=J)
       c_(k,i,j) binom(I,i)/binom(d,i)
                   binom(J,j)/binom(e,j).              (10)

This follows by expanding `t^i` and `u^j` in their respective Bernstein
bases. A polynomial whose coefficients in (10) are nonnegative is
nonnegative for `x>=0,0<=t,u<=1`, since all the basis polynomials are
nonnegative. Constants and absent variables use degree zero.

For P0 after (9), the minimum Bernstein coefficient at each successive
x degree `k=0,1,2,3` is

    65/9,  161/9,  25/9,  1/9.                         (11)

For P, use the following five rectangles. In every row its t,u degrees
are four and two. The entries are the minima of (10), over
`0<=I<=4,0<=J<=2`, at the successive x degrees `k=0,...,4`:

| t interval | u interval | k=0 | k=1 | k=2 | k=3 | k=4 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [0,1/4] | [0,1/2] | 4904269/9216 | 1345403/6912 | 24071/768 | 7715/3456 | 221/3456 |
| [1/4,1/2] | [0,1/2] | 6713755/13824 | 1617115/6912 | 196775/4608 | 8057/2304 | 8051/82944 |
| [0,1/2] | [1/2,1] | 496429/864 | 196495/864 | 10501/288 | 2317/864 | 1/16 |
| [1/2,1] | [0,1/2] | 99693/64 | 20861/32 | 807/8 | 219/32 | 11/64 |
| [1/2,1] | [1/2,1] | 61281/64 | 5867/16 | 1677/32 | 53/16 | 5/64 |

For clarity, each table entry is obtained solely by substituting (9) into
(6) or (7), applying the affine rectangle substitution to t,u, expanding,
and using (10). Thus the table specifies an independently reproducible
finite coefficient certificate, not a sampled sign test. All entries are
positive, and the five rectangles cover the whole unit square. This proves
`P0>0,P>0` for `L>=11` in the required ranges.

For the remaining integer values `2<=L<=10`, substitute every integer a
with `1<=a<=L-1` and `L-1<=3a<2L+1` into P0, and every integer
`1<=j<=a` into P. The number of entries and their minimum are:

| L | entries | minimum |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2 | 2 | 0 |
| 3 | 5 | 0 |
| 4 | 5 | 0 |
| 5 | 7 | 0 |
| 6 | 12 | 12 |
| 7 | 12 | 18 |
| 8 | 15 | 76 |
| 9 | 22 | 54 |
| 10 | 22 | 72 |

All formulas here are integral polynomials, so this last finite table uses
only integer substitutions. It completes the residual inequalities for all
cone generators. Summing them proves the right side of (1). Reflection
proves the left side, and the explicit `(4,3,2,1)` example proves sharpness.

## 5. Consequence for a true-centroid cap with only one proper fiber

Consider any finite consecutive family of positive intervals
`K_i=[l_i,r_i]`, with convex lower and concave upper endpoint sequences.
Assume its true, unweighted mixed-length centroid is `(0,0)`. Thus

    w_i=r_i-l_i,  sum_i i w_i=0,
    Q:=sum_i w_i^2,  sum_i w_i r_i=Q/2.

Jensen for r at the integer mean gives `r_0>=Q/(2M)>0`; Jensen for l
similarly gives `l_0<=-Q/(2M)<0`. In particular the anchor is proper.

Suppose a nonvertical cap through the centroid has, after a lattice-
preserving shear and possibly reflection, equation `x>=0`, its only
properly cut fiber is i=0, and it has no endpoint coincidences. Suppose
also that at least one of its two outer tails is wholly captured. Its
actual cap mass F is `r_0+T`, where T is the mass of its captured tails.
By (1), whether one or both tails are captured,

    T>= (3/7)(M-w_0).

Writing `p=w_0/M` and using `Q/M^2>=p^2`, we obtain

    F/M >= (3/7)(1-p)+p^2/2
         =33/98+(p-3/7)^2/2 >=33/98>1/3.              (12)

The strict gap above one third is `1/294`. This includes arbitrarily many
positive fibers and asymmetric base supports. It does not treat symmetric
proper blocks containing three or more fibers. The exact angular reduction
in `candidate bca993ec81e97cb4` shows that those
larger blocks are the remaining captured-tail configurations for a universal
one-third theorem. No assertion about higher continuous dimensions or full
(OC) is made here.
